### Problem: Superultra's Favorite Permutation {#sec-part-p4-b}

::: {.p-statement}
For each test case ($t \le 10^4$, $2 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$, sum of $n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$), construct a permutation $p$ of $1..n$ such that **every adjacent sum** $p_i + p_{i+1}$ is composite, or print $-1$ if none exists. (Composite = has a divisor besides $1$ and itself; $4$ counts, $1$ is neither prime nor composite but no adjacent sum here can be $1$ or below.)

Source: [CF 2037C · Superultra's Favorite Permutation](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/2037/C){.solved rating="1000"}

Example: `n = 8` → `1 8 7 3 6 2 4 5` (one valid answer; any permutation passes). `n = 3` → `-1`.
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Partition by parity. Two numbers of the same parity have an even sum, and every even sum here is at least $1 + 3 = 4$, hence composite; so inside an all-even block and an all-odd block every neighbour pair is safe. Only the one **seam** between the blocks (even $+$ odd, an odd sum) can be prime. Make it a multiple of $3$: if the even block ends with $E$, start the odd block with the odd $o \in \{1, 3, 5\}$ that has $E + o \equiv 0 \pmod 3$; then $E + o \ge 9$ is composite. This needs $5 \le n$; for $n \le 4$ no answer exists.
:::

This is the wiggle problem (@sec-part-p4-a) turned around: there a partition around the median made every neighbour comparison safe except where copies of one value meet; here a partition by parity makes every neighbour sum safe except at one seam. In both, the work is in the one place where the two groups touch.

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Exhaustive scan (brute).** Try all $n!$ permutations, test every adjacent sum. Exact, tiny only; it is what tells us $n \in \{2,3,4\}$ are the impossible cases.
2. **Evens ascending, odds ascending, head $= 1$.** $O(n)$ construction; the seam sum is $E + 1$. Works exactly when $E + 1$ is composite — e.g. $n = 8$: seam $9$, valid; $n = 6$: seam $7$, prime, invalid. Shows *where* a naive construction breaks.
3. **Residue-chosen odd head (optimal).** Same blocks, but the first odd is the one with $o \equiv -E \pmod 3$ (always exists in $\{1,3,5\}$). Every internal sum composite by parity, the seam by divisibility with $3$; $O(n)$, correct for all $n \ge 5$, $-1$ otherwise.

**Proof (form 3).** (i) Inside the even block, sums are even and at least $2 + 4 = 6$. (ii) Inside the odd block, sums are even and at least $1 + 3 = 4$. (iii) The seam $E + o$ is a multiple of $3$ and at least $4 + 5 = 9$ when $E = 4$, or at least $6 + 3 = 9$ otherwise; a multiple of $3$ above $3$ is composite. The three residues mod $3$ are $1 \equiv 1$, $5 \equiv 2$, $3 \equiv 0$, so the right head always exists once $n \ge 5$. For $n \in \{2, 3, 4\}$ the exhaustive scan finds nothing. $\blacksquare$
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Exhaustive scan

::: {.form-next}
Enumerate permutations in lexicographic order and test all $n-1$ adjacent sums. On $n = 3$ (official sample) all six fail — the note's claim, machine-checked — which is also how we established that only $n \in \{2,3,4\}$ are impossible.
:::

    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("superultra", "brute")
    assert str(final) == "-1"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)

##### Python

```{python}
import itertools


def is_composite(x):
    return x == 4 or (x > 4 and any(x % d == 0 for d in range(2, int(x ** 0.5) + 1)))


def superultra_brute(n):
    for perm in itertools.permutations(range(1, n + 1)):
        if all(is_composite(perm[i] + perm[i + 1]) for i in range(n - 1)):
            return list(perm)
    return None


assert superultra_brute(2) is None
assert superultra_brute(3) is None
assert superultra_brute(4) is None
assert superultra_brute(5) is not None
print("superultra_brute OK: -1 exactly for n in {2,3,4}")
```

#### Evens ascending, odds ascending, head 1

::: {.form-next}
Commit to the parity split: `2, 4, ..., E`, then `1`, then the other odds. Internal sums are safe; only the seam $E + 1$ needs luck. On $n = 8$ the seam is $9$ and the construction works; on $n = 6$ (traced below) it is $7$, a prime. The failure says exactly what form 3 must control.
:::

```{python}

#| renderings: [light, dark]

    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("superultra", "evens")
    assert str(final) == "seam 7 is prime: invalid"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

##### Python

```{python}
def superultra_head1(n):
    evens = list(range(2, n + 1, 2))
    odds = [o for o in range(1, n + 1, 2) if o != 1]
    return evens + [1] + odds


res8 = superultra_head1(8)
assert res8 == [2, 4, 6, 8, 1, 3, 5, 7]
assert all(is_composite(res8[i] + res8[i + 1]) for i in range(7))  # seam 8+1 = 9

res6 = superultra_head1(6)
assert not all(is_composite(res6[i] + res6[i + 1]) for i in range(5))  # seam 6+1 = 7
print("head-1 construction: ok at n=8, seam prime at n=6")
```

##### C++

```cpp
// fragment - head-1 construction; same single seam to check.
#include <vector>
using namespace std;
vector<int> superultraHead1(int n) {
    vector<int> p;
    for (int v = 2; v <= n; v += 2) p.push_back(v);
    p.push_back(1);
    for (int v = 3; v <= n; v += 2) p.push_back(v);
    return p;
}
```

:::

#### Residue-chosen odd head

::: {.form-next}
Keep the blocks, stop relying on luck. The seam value $o$ must satisfy $E + o \equiv 0 \pmod 3$ — one of the three residues, and $\{1, 3, 5\}$ contains an odd for *every* residue class. Pick it as the head of the odd block. For $n \ge 5$ the head exists and the seam is $\ge 9$; for $n < 5$ print $-1$.
:::

```{python}

#| renderings: [light, dark]

    assert str(final) == "[2, 4, 6, 3, 1, 5]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

##### Python

```{python}
def superultra(n):
    if n < 5:
        return None
    evens = list(range(2, n + 1, 2))
    r = (-evens[-1]) % 3                    # seam needs (E + o) % 3 == 0
    odds = list(range(1, n + 1, 2))
    head = next(o for o in odds if o % 3 == r)   # always found in {1, 3, 5}
    return evens + [head] + [o for o in odds if o != head]


for n in range(5, 300):
    p = superultra(n)
    assert sorted(p) == list(range(1, n + 1))
    assert all(is_composite(p[i] + p[i + 1]) for i in range(n - 1)), n
assert superultra(6) == [2, 4, 6, 3, 1, 5]   # the board sample
# cross-check the impossible set against the exhaustive oracle
for n in range(2, 8):
    assert (superultra(n) is None) == (superultra_brute(n) is None), n
print("superultra OK for n = 5..299; the impossible set matches the brute force")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

vector<int> superultra(int n) {          // empty vector = impossible
    if (n < 5) return {};
    vector<int> p;
    int lastEven = n % 2 == 0 ? n : n - 1;
    for (int v = 2; v <= lastEven; v += 2) p.push_back(v);
    int r = (3 - lastEven % 3) % 3;
    int head = (r == 0) ? 3 : (r == 1) ? 1 : 5;   // 3|E -> 3, E%3=2 -> 1, E%3=1 -> 5
    p.push_back(head);
    for (int v = 1; v <= n; v += 2)
        if (v != head) p.push_back(v);
    return p;
}

int main() {
    for (int n : {3, 5, 6, 8}) {
        vector<int> p = superultra(n);
        if (p.empty()) { cout << "-1\n"; continue; }
        for (size_t i = 0; i < p.size(); ++i) cout << p[i] << " \n"[i + 1 == p.size()];
    }
    return 0;
}
```

:::
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Exhaustive scan**: $O(n! \cdot n)$, an oracle only. **Evens ascending, odds ascending, head 1**: $O(n)$, but wrong whenever $E + 1$ is prime. **Residue-chosen odd head**: $O(n)$ per test, $O(\sum n)$ in total, correct for every $n \ge 5$.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- **$n = 2, 3, 4$**: print $-1$. By hand: for $n = 4$ the only composite pair sums are $1 + 3 = 4$ and $2 + 4 = 6$, two disjoint pairs that no third composite sum can join into a path of four; smaller $n$ have even fewer.
- **$n = 5$** (smallest feasible): $E = 4$, $r = 2$, head $= 5$ — result $[2, 4, 5, 1, 3]$: seam $9$, then $5+1=6$, $1+3=4$.
- **The head is at most $5$**: $1, 3, 5$ cover the three residues mod $3$, and all three exist because $n \ge 5$.
- **The pair after the head**: head $+$ next odd is an odd $+$ odd sum, even and at least $1 + 3 = 4$, so composite.
:::

::: {.practice}
- [CF 1352G · Special Permutation](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1352/G){rating="1600"} — neighbours must differ by $2$, $3$ or $4$: odds descending, evens ascending, and again only the seam between the two parity blocks needs a hand-picked pair.
:::
